questions.question: Three enterprise accounts asked for meeting summaries through one account manager in one month. Which conclusion does this evidence actually support?
options: Enterprise team leads lose decisions after recurring meetings often enough to justify roadmap capacity
At least three accounts reached by this account manager articulated a want for meeting summaries in that month
Meeting summaries are the highest-value unmet need in the enterprise segment
Enterprise customers will churn without meeting summaries
questions.explanation: The evidence establishes that the want was expressed, by whom, through what channel, and when — nothing further. A is the tempting distractor because it sounds like a measured version of the same thing, but it asserts prevalence, and requests arriving through one channel are not a sample. Frequency of asking is not frequency of happening.

questions.question: A PM writes: "Enterprise customers need automated meeting summaries." Which single edit removes the most unearned weight?
options: Change "need" to "would benefit from", to soften the strength of the claim
Add the roughly 20% revenue figure, so readers can see the stakes
Replace "enterprise customers" with "three accounts, all reached through one account manager in January"
Add a footnote pointing to the account manager's call notes
questions.explanation: The category name is what turns three cases into a population, and it is the piece that survives every downstream summary. C puts population, count, channel and window into the sentence itself. D is the tempting distractor: a footnote is stripped off in the first re-quote, which is exactly how the limit becomes invisible.

questions.question: The case states that the underlying claim — enterprise team leads repeatedly lose decisions and context after recurring meetings — has never been tested. How should this fact be handled?
options: As a neutral gap to note in an appendix while proceeding with the request as stated
As a reason to discard the signal, since untested claims cannot inform a roadmap
As the largest single fact in the signal: the mechanism behind the request is unverified, so the request cannot stand in for the problem
As a task for analytics to close by segmenting meeting-related events
questions.explanation: Everything the request implies about value depends on a mechanism nobody has checked, so the untested status is load-bearing rather than incidental. D is tempting and quietly impossible: the case states meeting type is not captured at all, so analytics cannot close this gap by segmentation.

questions.question: The three requesting accounts represent roughly 20% of current revenue. What does that figure establish?
options: That the problem is widespread among high-value customers
That the expected value of building summaries exceeds the expected value of the alternatives
That the requests are more likely to be accurate descriptions of the underlying work
The size of the commercial consequence attached to these accounts — not anything about whether the problem is real or common
questions.explanation: Contract value measures what is at stake with these accounts. It says nothing about prevalence, mechanism, or accuracy. A is the tempting distractor because revenue concentration feels like it multiplies the evidence, when it only multiplies the consequence of being wrong in either direction.

questions.question: A PM starts writing population, window, source and limit next to every sentence in every document. What is wrong with this?
options: The discipline is for load-bearing claims; applied to everything it produces unread documents and protects no decision
Nothing — full bounding is the standard the lesson sets
Bounding should be done by the analytics team, not the PM
The four fields belong in a research repository rather than in planning documents
questions.explanation: This is the boundary of the model. The purpose is to protect claims that decisions rest on; background context gains nothing and costs attention. D is tempting because a repository sounds tidier, but moving the fields away from the claim is the exact failure the lesson describes — a limit that does not travel with the sentence stops existing.
